outcome: Nothing since 26 January 2024 settles, bounds or moves the question. The only in-window item is a Lean formalisation of the open statement (merged 17 Oct 2025, proof body sorry), which proves nothing. The only partial result found is a square-divisor bound (any square dividing p#+1 exceeds 2.5×10^15), recorded by OEIS as coming from Vardi’s 1991 book and predating the window; Wikipedia still lists the question as open.
problem_asks: One universal yes/no claim: every Euclid number is square-free. (a) The family: the bullet gives no formula; the article it links to defines the n-th Euclid number as E_n = p_n# + 1, the product of the first n primes plus one. (b) The property: square-free, meaning no square m² with m > 1 divides E_n, equivalently no prime q has q² dividing E_n. (c) The quantifier: for all n, with no restriction on n, on the prime q, or on size. Not asked by this bullet: whether Euclid numbers are prime (a separate bullet on infinitely many Euclid primes), a bound on the size of any square factor, or the full factorisation of any E_n.

events.what_happened: Ilan Vardi, Computational Recreations in Mathematica (Addison-Wesley, 1991), sections 5.1–5.2, pp. 82–89, the chapter ‘Are All Euclid Numbers Squarefree?’. OEIS A054988 cites p. 87 for the statement ‘Any square dividing p#+1 must exceed 2.5*10^15’. I could not open the book, so the statement and its page are known only through that citation. MathWorld’s Sylvester’s-sequence entry attributes the same 2.5×10^15 figure to Vardi 1991 for a different sequence (no term below that bound is non-squarefree). This is the only partial result on the question I found.
events.delivers: Per the OEIS reading (not checked against the book): for every Euclid number, any square factor q² satisfies q² > 2.5×10^15, so no prime q below about 5×10^7 divides any E_n twice. The source does not state the method or range. My inference, not stated by the source: since q² | E_n forces q > p_n, the check is over the finitely many pairs (n, q) with p_n < q < 5×10^7, so it would cover every n at once.
events.remains: Every prime q above about 5×10^7, for every n. The universal claim that every E_n is square-free is untouched.
events.directly_checkable: Any single E_n can be checked for square factors by factoring it, or by testing p_n# ≡ −1 (mod q²) for each prime q with p_n < q. The bound is a claim over all n, so no single object is checkable. I did not run any check.
events.doubts: The only support is a one-line OEIS citation to a book page I could not read. OEIS gives no method, range or computation. MathWorld attaches the same 2.5×10^15 figure to Sylvester’s sequence, citing the same Vardi chapter, so the OEIS entry alone does not show whether the bound is for Euclid numbers, Sylvester’s sequence, or both. Nothing I found contradicts it.
events.direction: Partial, and cuts toward the conjecture: it excludes square factors below about 2.5×10^15 for every Euclid number, if the attribution holds. It does not decide the universal claim.

events.what_happened: Sean A. Irvine adds comments to OEIS A054988 (‘Number of prime divisors of 1 + (product of first n primes), with multiplicity’) dated 21 Oct 2023. He states that it is an open question whether omega(p#+1) = bigomega(p#+1) = a(n), that is, whether the Euclid numbers are squarefree, and repeats the 2.5×10^15 bound with the citation ‘see Vardi, p. 87’. No new computation is described.
events.delivers: Restates the open status and the same partial bound as the Vardi 1991 event. Adds no new mathematics or computation.
events.remains: The same as the Vardi 1991 event: every prime q above about 5×10^7 for every n, and the universal claim as a whole.
events.doubts: Relies wholly on the Vardi citation. Gives no computation, method or range.
events.direction: Same as the Vardi 1991 event: restates a partial result that cuts toward the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Nick Lord, ‘Euclid numbers are free from powers’, The Mathematical Gazette 98(543), 2014, pp. 482–483 (note 98.21; DOI 10.1017/S0025557200008184). Wikipedia cites it for the claim that no Euclid or Kummer number is a perfect power. This is a neighbouring result: it concerns perfect powers, not square divisors. The Cambridge Core page is paywalled and I did not read the note; the claim is taken from Wikipedia’s citation.
events.revisions: Cambridge Core lists the issue as November 2014 and online publication as 25 Aug 2015. I found no earlier preprint.
events.delivers: As cited by Wikipedia: no Euclid number (or Kummer number) is a perfect power x^k with k ≥ 2. This says nothing about whether q² divides E_n, since a non-perfect-power can still have a square factor. Discounted for this question.

checked_by.qualification: Refereed mathematics journal of record (Mathematical Association); I did not verify its refereeing for this note
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the note (online 25 Aug 2015 per Cambridge Core)

events.direction: Neighbouring: no Euclid number is a perfect power. It does not bear on square-freeness.

events.what_happened: Google DeepMind’s Formal Conjectures repository adds FormalConjectures/Wikipedia/Euclid.lean through PR #1123, ‘Formalization of the open problems about Euclid numbers’, which fixes issue #1122 ‘Euclid Numbers’. The PR was opened 15 Oct 2025 by szabadka, with a co-author trailer naming Moritz Firsching, and approved by callesonne and mo271; it was merged 17 Oct 2025 (commit 4d74786). The file defines Euclid n := 1 + ∏ i ∈ Finset.range n, i.nth Nat.Prime, and states theorem euclid_numbers_are_square_free : answer(sorry) ↔ (∀ n, Squarefree (Euclid n)) := by sorry. The docstring reads ‘It is not known whether every Euclid number is a square-free number.’, and the attribute is @[category research open, AMS 11]. The Lean text came through WebFetch extraction, not a raw copy.
events.revisions: PR opened 15 Oct 2025; merged 17 Oct 2025 (commit 4d74786). The commit list shows a later commit on 18 Sep 2026, ‘chore: modulize FormalConjectures/ (#4688)’, a restructuring commit whose effect on the file’s content I did not check.
events.delivers: No mathematical content toward the answer. It fixes the statement: E_n = 1 + (product of the first n primes), and the claim that all E_n are square-free, stated as an open conjecture with truth value answer(sorry). The proof body is sorry.

disputes.summary: The 2.5×10^15 square-divisor bound is attributed by OEIS A054988 to Euclid numbers, citing Vardi 1991 p. 87. MathWorld’s Sylvester’s-sequence entry gives the same 2.5×10^15 figure, citing Vardi 1991 without a page, for Sylvester’s sequence. I could not read the Vardi chapter, so it is unresolved whether the figure applies to Euclid numbers, to Sylvester’s sequence, or to both.

summary: I ran 48 web searches (verbatim in search.queries) and opened the current Wikipedia Euclid number article (last edited 9 Nov 2025; still lists the question as open), OEIS A006862, A054988 and A189409, MathWorld’s Euclid number and Sylvester’s sequence entries, the Booker–Pomerance paper (arXiv 1607.01557, via ar5iv), the Formal Conjectures file Euclid.lean with its PR #1123 and commit log, the Epoch FrontierMath Open Problems list (9 of about 49 entries visible), the AIM ‘AI and Number Theory’ 2026 workshop page, and the AlphaEvolve paper (arXiv 2511.02864, read through about section 26). The events are: a 1991 partial bound (no square factor below 2.5×10^15), restated by Irvine in OEIS in Oct 2023; a 2014 note showing no Euclid number is a perfect power, which is neighbouring and discounted; and a Lean formalisation of the open statement, merged 17 Oct 2025 with a sorry body. Nothing in the window moves the problem. Close calls: (a) the 1991 bound is recorded as an event but predates the window, and its attribution rests on one OEIS citation to a book page I could not read, with a second source attaching the same figure to Sylvester’s sequence; (b) the Lean formalisation is recorded because it is a formal bearing on the problem, though it contains no mathematics toward the answer. Booker and Pomerance (2016/2017) state three open questions in their Section 6, none about Euclid numbers, so their paper is not an event. Campbell’s 2026 arXiv 2609.14714 and the Lee–O’Clarey 2026 preprint concern prime plus non-squarefree integers, not Euclid numbers, and are dead ends. AI: I found no source connecting any AI system to this problem; ai.none_found is true for every event. The AI-credited results I saw (Erdős problems #848, #728, #11 and #1196, the unit-distance counterexample, the Carlitz–Wieferich preprint arXiv 2607.15305 naming ‘Claude Opus 4.8’, and the AlphaEvolve paper) concern other questions. Of those, I opened only the AlphaEvolve paper and the AI4Math survey arXiv 2608.24961 (abstract only); the rest are search snippets. The AlphaEvolve text I read through about section 26 has no Euclid or primorial hit; sections 27–35 were not read. Heuristic, not sourced: since E_n is coprime to every prime up to p_n, a square factor needs q > p_n, and the expected count of such q is about the sum over q > p_n of 1/q², which is roughly 1/(p_n log p_n) and summable over n. That suggests non-square-free Euclid numbers are rare, but it is my own derivation and gives no evidence either way for the universal claim.
competing_reading: Read one way, the record is a clean ‘nothing happened’: the only in-window item is a statement formalisation with sorry, and the only partial result predates the window and rests on one citation. Read another way, a 1991 bound that rules out every square factor below 2.5×10^15 for all Euclid numbers is a real restriction that a fair reader could count as partial progress, not just background. A third reading treats the Lean statement as the most authoritative current formulation, which would make the problem’s status ‘open, formally stated’. I record the bound as a predating event and do not rank these readings.
what_would_settle_it: (1) Vardi 1991 pp. 82–89 (§§5.1–5.2), to confirm the bound’s scope, method and whether it is for Euclid numbers, Sylvester’s sequence, or both. (2) Any published or OEIS computation stating the range of n and q that was checked for square factors of E_n. (3) A verified square factor of some E_n, which would answer the question negatively, or a proof for all n, which would answer it positively. (4) For AI involvement: a lab, benchmark or tracker entry that names this problem with a system and quotes the authors’ own account; none was found, and the Formal Conjectures statement carries no AI attribution.
